---

## Physics Requirements Analysis

**Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at ALL angles including 90° and backward:**
- Tracks going transverse or backward never reach the downstream drift chambers
- Need tracking coverage that is essentially 4π around the interaction vertex
- Tracks must be identified even when very short or curling in the field

**Recoiling protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy:**
- 60 MeV proton range in liquid/solid material: ~a few mm to ~1 cm
- These are very short tracks — need fine-grained 3D tracking
- Must distinguish protons from pions (particle ID)

**Hydrogen ≤2% of target nucleons:**
- Rules out water (H₂O: ~11% H by nucleon count)
- Rules out hydrocarbon scintillator (CH: ~50% H)
- Rules out liquid argon (no hydrogen, fine) but LAr has its own constraints
- Favors argon, carbon with minimal hydrogen, or similar heavy noble/inert targets
- This is the most chemically restrictive requirement

---

## Hardware Upgrades

### 1. High-Pressure Gaseous Argon Time Projection Chamber (HPgTPC) as Active Target

**Technology:** High-pressure (≥10 atm) gaseous argon TPC filling the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m target volume, with multi-wire or GEM/micropattern readout planes.

**Why:**
- Argon is a noble gas — zero hydrogen content, satisfying the ≤2% hydrogen constraint with margin
- At 10 atm, density ~18 kg/m³, giving adequate neutrino interaction rate while maintaining low enough density that 60 MeV protons (range ~a few cm at 10 atm) are fully tracked within the volume
- 3D continuous tracking provides low detection threshold for short recoil proton tracks
- Fine spatial resolution (order mm) from TPC drift enables reconstruction of very short tracks (~1–2 cm) from 60 MeV protons
- Isotropic sensitivity: a TPC records tracks at all angles, including 90° transverse and backward-going tracks, satisfying the muon angular coverage requirement without geometric gaps
- The drift field can be tuned; with cathode and anode planes on the upstream/downstream faces, transverse tracks are fully imaged

**Specific sub-components needed:**
- High-voltage cathode plane (upstream face) and anode readout plane (downstream face) with GEM or MicroMegas amplification stages
- Field cage surrounding the drift volume
- High-pressure vessel rated to ≥10 atm enclosing the active volume
- Gas recirculation and purification system (O₂, H₂O contamination must be <1 ppb for long drift)
- Front-end electronics on the anode plane with low-noise charge amplifiers, capable of resolving ~1 mm pitch pads

---

### 2. Scintillator Barrel / Surrounding Veto and Containment Detector

**Technology:** Extruded plastic scintillator bars with WLS fiber readout and SiPM photodetectors, arranged as a barrel around the TPC pressure vessel on the four sides not covered by the upstream beam face and downstream magnet exit.

**Why:**
- Muons and pions leaving the TPC at large angles (approaching 90°) exit the pressure vessel laterally; matching TPC tracks to the scintillator barrel provides momentum measurement by range for tracks that stop in the barrel, and confirms the exit direction of tracks that escape
- Provides a veto/tagging layer to reject cosmic ray backgrounds and to tag events where a particle exits the active target — necessary for the efficiency requirement at all angles
- Plastic scintillator is fast (ns timing) and inexpensive for large area coverage
- SiPMs are compact, operable within the stray field of the warm dipole
- WLS fiber readout allows long bars with single-ended or double-ended readout
- Bars can be oriented in alternating X–Y layers to provide 2D position resolution at the barrel surface for track matching

**Note on hydrogen in scintillator:** The scintillator barrel surrounds but is not inside the defined 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m target volume, so its hydrogen content does not violate the ≤2% nucleon constraint provided the analysis fiducial volume is restricted to the TPC gas. The hydrogen-removal model applies to the target volume only.

---

### 3. Upstream Beam Monitor / Anti-coincidence Plane

**Technology:** Two planes of thin (3 mm) plastic scintillator with SiPM readout placed immediately upstream of the target volume, covering the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m face.

**Why:**
- Identifies charged particles (muons, pions, halo protons) entering the target from upstream in the beam, allowing rejection of beam-induced backgrounds that would otherwise fake neutrino interactions
- Provides a timing reference (neutrino beam spill structure is ~µs; in-spill cosmics and beam halo must be vetoed)
- Thin enough not to introduce significant material or hydrogen before the active target
- Two planes separated by ~5 cm give a direction estimate for penetrating tracks

---

### 4. Downstream Muon Catcher / Range Stack Upgrade

**Technology:** Additional planes of iron absorber (5–10 cm slabs) interleaved with scintillator strips, added immediately downstream of the existing drift chambers, with updated SiPM readout replacing any existing PMTs.

**Why:**
- Forward-going muons that exit the TPC downstream and pass through the existing drift chambers may have momenta too high to be fully measured by the 0.15 T, 6.5 m dipole alone (maximum measurable momentum ~1.5 GeV/c for 25% uncertainty); a range stack extends momentum measurement by ranging out higher-energy muons
- More critically, forward muons that punch through the entire spectrometer need to be identified as muons (not pions) — iron + scintillator provides muon/pion separation by range and by characteristic energy deposition
- SiPM replacement of PMTs improves reliability, reduces operating voltage, and provides operation in residual magnetic field regions near the dipole fringe

---

### 5. TPC Readout Electronics and DAQ Upgrade

**Technology:** Continuous streaming readout ASICs (e.g., SAMPA-class or equivalent) with zero-suppression in firmware, coupled to an FPGA-based DAQ capable of recording full waveforms during the beam spill window, with online track-finding trigger.

**Why:**
- A high-pressure TPC with fine pad pitch over ~6 m² of anode area generates very large data volumes; existing DAQ infrastructure designed for the original (non-TPC) target cannot handle this
- The neutrino beam spill (~10 µs) requires the entire drift time window (~100 µs for a ~50 cm maximum drift at typical drift velocities of ~5 cm/µs at 10 atm) to be recorded without deadtime
- Online trigger must select neutrino interaction candidates before writing to permanent storage; offline reconstruction of 60 MeV proton tracks requires full waveform information, not simple hit lists
- Streaming readout avoids trigger efficiency biases that would undermine the ≥25% efficiency requirement at all angles

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target TPC | High-pressure gaseous argon TPC with GEM/MicroMegas readout | 60 MeV proton tracking; 4π muon coverage; ≤2% hydrogen |
| Surrounding barrel detector | Extruded scintillator + WLS fiber + SiPM | Muon containment/range at large angles |
| Upstream veto planes | Thin scintillator + SiPM | Beam background rejection |
| Downstream muon catcher | Iron/scintillator range stack + SiPM | High-momentum forward muon ID and measurement |
| Readout electronics & DAQ | Streaming ASIC + FPGA DAQ | Low-threshold track reconstruction; no trigger bias |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target with a high-pressure gaseous argon time projection chamber, as it simultaneously satisfies all three hardest constraints — zero hydrogen content, 4π tracking acceptance for muons at all angles including backward, and millimeter-scale 3D resolution sufficient to reconstruct 60 MeV recoil proton tracks — none of which can be achieved with any other single technology choice.

# Design Review Recommendations: Kestrel Flats Near Station Active Target Upgrade

## Analysis of Requirements

Before recommending hardware, let me work through the constraints systematically.

**Magnetic analysis:** 0.15 T over 6.5 m gives a bending power of Bρ → maximum sagitta analysis. For a track fully contained in the magnet, the momentum resolution is adequate for muons above ~150 MeV/c. The critical issue is **angular acceptance**: tracks perpendicular to the beam axis travel along the drift direction of downstream chambers and are essentially undetected by them. Backward-going tracks never reach those chambers at all.

**Hydrogen constraint:** ≤2% hydrogen nucleons means the active target material must be predominantly heavy nuclei. Pure hydrocarbon scintillator (CH₂ or similar) is disqualified. Water (H₂O) gives ~11% hydrogen by nucleon count — also disqualified. Liquid argon gives 0% hydrogen. Carbon gives 0%. The constraint strongly favors nuclear targets with no or minimal hydrogen.

**Proton tracking:** 60 MeV kinetic energy protons have a range in water of ~1.6 mm and in plastic scintillator of ~1.4 mm. This demands **millimeter-scale or sub-millimeter spatial resolution** throughout the active target volume.

**Volume:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m = ~5.4 m³ is a large active volume at this granularity.

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. Replace the passive target with a 3D-granular plastic scintillator tracker — but with carbon-rich, low-hydrogen tiles read out via SiPMs (Super-FGD style)

**Technology:** Segmented scintillator cubes (~1 cm³) with three-axis wavelength-shifting fiber readout and SiPM photodetectors, following the SuperFGD concept demonstrated for T2K.

**Justification:**
- 1 cm cube pitch gives ~1 cm³ voxels, providing sufficient resolution to reconstruct proton tracks down to ~3–4 cm range (60 MeV kinetic energy protons range ~3 cm in scintillator), meeting the low-energy proton requirement.
- Three-axis fiber readout gives full 4π angular acceptance with no preferred track direction, directly solving the perpendicular and backward-track efficiency requirement. Unlike planar detectors, there is no dead angle.
- Scintillator (polystyrene, C₈H₈) has a hydrogen fraction of ~7.7% by nucleon number — **this exceeds the 2% constraint**. However, see mitigation below.
- Fast timing (~1 ns) from SiPMs allows neutron rejection and track-direction disambiguation for backward-going tracks.
- The technology is mature: T2K's SuperFGD is commissioned; the collaboration can adopt validated cube geometry and readout.

**Hydrogen mitigation for scintillator:** The 2% cap cannot be met with pure polystyrene. This drives recommendation 2.

---

### 2. Replace scintillator cubes with a Liquid Argon or solid argon / carbon-based target interspersed with thin active layers — or adopt a **carbon-slab + emulsion cloud chamber (ECC) with NINJA-style active layers**

**Revised primary technology: Carbon target with thin scintillating fiber (SciFi) tracker planes**

**Technology:** Alternating passive carbon plates (graphite or carbon-fiber composite, ~1–2 radiation lengths thick) interleaved with **scintillating fiber tracker planes** (250–500 µm diameter fibers, SiPM readout) in X and Y projections, with ~1 cm plate spacing.

**Justification:**
- Carbon (¹²C) contains **zero free hydrogen**; hydrogen nucleon fraction = 0%. This satisfies the ≤2% constraint with large margin.
- SciFi planes at 250 µm pitch achieve the spatial resolution needed: a 60 MeV proton ranges ~3 cm in carbon (density ~2.2 g/cm³), giving ~15–30 measurable hits across planes before stopping — reconstructable with high efficiency.
- The sandwich geometry still provides 4π angular coverage as long as plate spacing is small compared to the shortest tracks of interest. At 1 cm spacing, a perpendicular proton track crosses multiple planes; a backward muon is tracked back through upstream planes.
- SciFi technology is proven at large scale (LHCb SciFi tracker); SiPM-based readout at the required channel count (~10⁵–10⁶ channels for this volume at 500 µm pitch) is commercially available and cost-effective.
- Carbon plates can be machined to exact dimensions; the passive material budget is well-controlled, aiding the neutrino cross-section modeling.

**Outstanding issue:** Gaps between carbon plates create dead zones for tracks parallel to the plates. Mitigate with **stereo-angle SciFi layers** (e.g., ±7°) and thin transverse (YZ-plane) scintillator strip layers at the upstream and downstream faces to catch parallel tracks.

---

### 3. Add a thin-wall time projection chamber (TPC) or μ-RWELL detector layer on the inner walls of the magnet bore surrounding the target

**Technology:** Micro-pattern gaseous detector (MPGD) panels — specifically **µ-RWELL or GEM-based** panels — lining the four lateral faces (top, bottom, and both sides) of the target region, with an argon:CO₂ drift gas.

**Justification:**
- Tracks leaving the target laterally (perpendicular or near-perpendicular to beam) exit through these faces. The SciFi/carbon sandwich alone gives reduced efficiency for such tracks because they may traverse only one or two plate-plane intersections.
- MPGD panels on the lateral faces provide a **dedicated perpendicular-track trigger and momentum seed**, achieving the required ≥25% reconstruction efficiency at 90° to the beam.
- µ-RWELL detectors are robust, operate at modest gas gain (10³–10⁴), and have been successfully deployed in environments with significant backgrounds. They are thin (a few mm), minimally perturbing the magnetic field.
- The spatial resolution of ~100 µm from these detectors, combined with the known magnetic field, enables standalone momentum measurement of tracks that do not reach the downstream drift chambers — the primary failure mode for perpendicular/backward tracks in the current design.
- Timing resolution of ~10 ns is sufficient to associate hits with the correct beam spill and to determine track direction (forward vs. backward) using drift time.

---

### 4. Upgrade the downstream gas drift chambers to operate in **high-rate mode with updated front-end electronics**

**Technology:** Replace the existing wire chamber front-end ASICs with radiation-hard, low-noise amplifier-shaper-discriminator chips (e.g., AFTER-based or DREAM-based chips as used in ND280/CALICE), and add **time-of-flight (ToF) scintillator panels** immediately downstream of the target exit face.

**Justification:**
- The existing drift chambers are designed for the original passive target occupancy. An active target reconstructing more interactions (and generating more secondary tracks) will increase hit rates; the existing electronics may saturate or suffer deadtime.
- A ToF panel (5–10 cm thick plastic scintillator, ~200 ps resolution) at the target exit disambiguates forward-going muons from backward-going ones that scatter and re-emerge, and provides a multiplicity trigger for the event.
- This is a relatively low-cost electronics upgrade that protects the existing momentum-measurement investment.

---

### 5. Install a **beam upstream veto and interaction trigger scintillator** at the upstream face of the target

**Technology:** One plane of 1 cm × 1 cm cross-section plastic scintillator bars with SiPM readout, spanning the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m upstream face.

**Justification:**
- Charged particles entering the target from upstream (beam halo muons, pion charge-exchange products from the target station) must be vetoed to avoid mis-identifying them as neutrino interaction products.
- The fine segmentation (1 cm bars) limits accidental veto rate while still providing charged-particle identification.
- This plane also serves as a **multiplicity trigger seed**: a single hit in the veto coincident with a downstream interaction vertex strongly indicates a beam neutrino candidate rather than a cosmic or beam-related background.
- SiPM readout matches the technology already adopted for the main active target, simplifying calibration and DAQ integration.

---

## Summary Table

| Change | Technology | Key Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target medium | Carbon plates + SciFi trackers | Hydrogen ≤2%, proton tracking to 60 MeV |
| Lateral coverage | µ-RWELL/GEM panels on target walls | ≥25% muon efficiency at 90° and backward |
| Downstream protection | ToF + upgraded drift chamber electronics | Forward muon momentum, rate capability |
| Upstream veto | Segmented scintillator plane | Background rejection, trigger |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target with alternating carbon-plate / scintillating-fiber sandwich planes read out by SiPMs, providing zero free hydrogen (satisfying the ≤2% nucleon constraint), millimeter-scale 3D tracking for 60 MeV protons, and full 4π angular acceptance for muon reconstruction including perpendicular and backward-going tracks.

# Proposed upgrade: a pixelated liquid-argon TPC active target, with side and upstream tracking

## 1. Why the target cannot be plastic or water

The hydrogen limit decides the target material before anything else.

| Target | Hydrogen fraction of nucleons | Meets the 2% limit? |
|---|---|---|
| Polystyrene scintillator, CH | 1/13 ≈ 7.7% | No |
| Water, H₂O | 2/18 ≈ 11% | No |
| Argon | 0% | Yes |

A fine-grained plastic-scintillator design (such as a SuperFGD-style cube target) is therefore excluded as the target material, even though it would otherwise meet the angular requirements. The far detector has no hydrogen, so an argon target also matches the far-detector nucleus, which is the natural choice.

## 2. Main change: modular liquid-argon TPC filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region

**Readout and modules**
- Use ArgonCube-style modules, about 1 × 1 m footprint, with optically segmented drift cells.
- Read the charge out on a pixel plane (LArPix-type cold ASICs, about 4 mm pitch) instead of wires. Pixels give unambiguous 3D reconstruction at every track angle, including tracks perpendicular to the beam and backward-going tracks. That directly serves the ≥25% muon efficiency requirement.

**Mass**
- The liquid-argon volume is about 5 m³, or roughly 7 t. That is ample for event rate at 410 m.

**Protons**
- A 60 MeV kinetic-energy proton travels about 3 cm in liquid argon, which is roughly 7 pixels at 4 mm pitch.
- Its Bragg peak is resolvable, so particle ID by dE/dx versus range works. Short protons are found at any angle because the readout is isotropic.

**Light detection**
- Add thin-profile light readout (ArCLight or light-collection-module tiles) on the field-cage walls of each optically isolated cell.
- This gives nanosecond event time, separates pile-up within a beam spill, and provides a start time (t₀) for each module.

**Orientation in the magnet**
- Align the drift field parallel to the 0.15 T dipole field, so there is no E×B distortion. If that is impossible, calibrate the distortion with a UV laser system.
- The 0.15 T field also curves contained tracks. Combined with multiple-Coulomb-scattering momentum estimates, this gives muon momentum and charge for tracks that never reach the downstream drift chambers.

**Cryostat**
- Use a thin-walled, low-Z membrane or aluminium-honeycomb vacuum-insulated cryostat. This keeps dead material small for tracks exiting toward the downstream drift chambers.
- Keep all hydrogenous insulation (foams) outside the fiducial volume.
- Select the fiducial volume by vertex position, so interactions in surrounding material are rejected.

## 3. Add tracking for high-angle and backward muons

The existing drift chambers sit only downstream, so muons leaving at large angles or backward would otherwise be lost.

- Install thin side and upstream tracker planes between the cryostat and the magnet yoke. Options are Ar/CO₂ drift or Micromegas/resistive-strip panels, or scintillator-bar planes; these are outside the target, so their hydrogen does not count.
- Add a few MRPC or fast-scintillator time-of-flight panels around the target to measure track direction (forward versus backward).
- Use an Ar/CO₂ gas mixture with no methane anywhere it could add to the target.
- Muons that stop in the argon are measured by range. Exiting muons are measured by curvature in the side trackers plus multiple scattering.

## 4. Alternative if cryogenics in the magnet is unacceptable

A high-pressure (around 10 bar) argon/CO₂ gas TPC would also contain no hydrogen and give excellent low-threshold protons.

Its drawback is mass: only about 90 kg in this volume, so the event rate is much lower. It is better treated as a complementary option than as the main target.

## 5. Calibration and support

- Purity monitors and argon recirculation and filtration, targeting electron lifetime above 2 ms.
- A UV laser for drift-field and E×B calibration.
- A cosmic-ray trigger for calibrating muon angular efficiency, including backward-going tracks.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a magnetized, pixel-readout (LArPix/ArgonCube-style) liquid-argon TPC active target, giving zero hydrogen, isotropic 3D tracking and a proton threshold of about 60 MeV kinetic energy.

This is an excellent design challenge for a near detector active target. Let me analyze the requirements and recommend specific solutions.

## Key Requirements Analysis

1. **Angular acceptance**: Need ≥25% efficiency for muons at ALL angles, including perpendicular and backward
2. **Low momentum protons**: Must detect protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~3 mm in plastic, ~1 cm in gas)
3. **Hydrogen constraint**: ≤2% of target nucleons can be hydrogen
4. **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m in 0.15 T field
5. **Flux**: Peak at 0.7 GeV neutrinos

## Critical Challenges with Current Setup

The existing gas drift chambers downstream cannot detect:
- Tracks perpendicular or backward to the beam (geometric acceptance)
- Very short proton tracks that stop in the target

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (SuperFGD-style)**

**Technology**: Extruded plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm³) with three-fold wavelength-shifting fiber readout and MPPC photosensors

**Justification**:
- 4π angular acceptance with true 3D tracking (X, Y, Z coordinates from orthogonal fiber orientations)
- Can reconstruct perpendicular and backward tracks that never reach downstream chambers
- ~1 cm granularity allows tracking of ~60 MeV protons (range ~2-3 cm in polystyrene)
- Proven technology (T2K ND280 upgrade, WAGASCI)
- Can operate in 0.15 T field (MPPCs are magnetic field tolerant)
- Timing resolution (~ns) enables vertex localization

**Specification**: ~200k cubes with ~600k fiber channels

### 2. **Low-Mass Target Material Selection: Carbon-Rich Composition**

**Technology**: Polystyrene-based scintillator (CH₁.₁) or specialized low-H formulation

**Justification**:
- Standard polystyrene: H/(C+H) = 1.1/2.1 = 52% by number, but accounting for neutrons: H makes ~14% of nucleons ✗ (too high)
- **Need custom formulation**: Target ~1.5% hydrogen by nucleon count
- Options:
  - Add high-Z loading (e.g., fluorinated polymers, but reduces light yield)
  - **Better**: Use primarily carbon-based target with minimal hydrogen
  - Consider segmented design with pure carbon layers + thin active layers

**Revised recommendation**: Hybrid approach with passive carbon plates + thin active layers

### 3. **Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Alternative/Hybrid**

**Technology**: Ar-based TPC with resistive Micromegas or GEM readout

**Justification**:
- Argon target: Zero hydrogen! (36Ar, 40Ar)
- Continuous 3D tracking with excellent spatial resolution (<1 mm)
- dE/dx measurement for particle ID (separate protons from pions)
- Can measure short proton tracks with multiple samples
- Proven in neutrino experiments (MicroBooNE, ND-GAr concept)
- Lower density than solid helps momentum resolution via range

**Challenges**: 
- Requires careful E-field design in 0.15 T magnetic field (parallel/perpendicular orientation critical)
- More complex, higher cost

### 4. **Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM/MPPC) Readout Upgrade**

**Technology**: High-density MPPC arrays with dedicated ASIC readout

**Justification**:
- Excellent timing (<1 ns) for beam-correlated events
- Compact, works in magnetic field
- Low voltage, radiation tolerant
- Essential for either scintillator or TPC option

### 5. **Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) Around Target Perimeter**

**Technology**: Timing RPCs on 4-5 faces of target volume

**Justification**:
- Catch sideways and backward-going muons immediately
- Excellent timing (<1 ns) for trigger and time-of-flight
- Low cost per area
- Complement 3D tracker for high-angle tracks
- Proven in neutrino experiments (OPERA, INO)

## Integrated Design Recommendation

**Primary solution**: **Hybrid Active Target**

1. **Core**: 3D scintillator tracker (SuperFGD-style) with 1 cm³ cubes
2. **Passive carbon plates** (2-5 cm thick) interspersed every 10-20 cm to increase target mass while minimizing hydrogen
3. **Resistive Micromegas TPC layers** (5-10 cm Ar gaps) between some carbon plates for enhanced particle ID
4. **RPC panels** on sides and rear face
5. All readout with modern SiPM + fast digitization ASICs

This gives:
- True 4π acceptance ✓
- ~1% hydrogen fraction achievable ✓
- Sufficient granularity for 60 MeV protons ✓
- Particle ID capability ✓
- Builds on proven technologies ✓

**Cost-optimized alternative**: SuperFGD + carbon plates + side/rear RPCs (defer TPC to Phase 2)

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a 3D fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker with three-fold fiber readout and MPPC photosensors (SuperFGD technology) to achieve true 4π angular acceptance and low-momentum proton detection capability

## Physics Requirements Analysis

**Geometry constraints:**
- Active target volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (transverse × transverse × longitudinal)
- Must reconstruct tracks at all angles including 90° and backward-going
- Muons: ≥25% efficiency at every angle
- Protons: down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range in water ~3.5 mm; in scintillator ~5 mm)

**60 MeV proton range estimates:**
- In liquid argon: ~4 mm
- In plastic scintillator (density ~1.03): ~5 mm
- In water: ~3.5 mm
- This sets the maximum granularity needed

**Hydrogen constraint:**
- H must be ≤2% of target nucleons by number
- Pure water: H is ~11% by mass, ~67% of nucleons — far too much
- Pure hydrocarbon (CH₂): H is ~14% by mass, ~50% of nucleons — far too much
- Pure carbon (graphite): 0% H — acceptable but not a practical active target alone
- Liquid argon: 0% H — fine, but see below
- The constraint effectively **rules out** water targets and pure plastic scintillator as the primary target material

**Hydrogen nucleon fraction calculation for polystyrene (C₈H₈):**
- H atoms per monomer: 8, C atoms: 8
- Nucleons: 8×1 + 8×12 = 8 + 96 = 104; H fraction = 8/104 ≈ 7.7% — too high

**For a composite target to get H ≤ 2%:**
- Must be predominantly high-A material
- E.g., iron or lead interleaved with thin active layers
- Or liquid argon (A=40, no H)
- Or a scintillator heavily loaded with high-Z material

**Beam and momentum measurement:**
- 0.7 GeV peak flux, near detector at 410 m: high rate environment
- Existing downstream drift chambers + 0.15 T dipole handle downstream-going tracks well
- Backward and perpendicular tracks do **not** exit into the downstream spectrometer — need momentum measurement within or around the active target itself

---

## Required Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Active Target: 3D Scintillator Cube Detector (plastic scintillator cubes with WLS fiber readout)

**Technology:** Array of ~1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes read out by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers along three orthogonal axes (SuperFGD-style), with SiPM photosensors.

**Why:**
- 1.5 cm cubes give sufficient granularity to detect ~60 MeV proton tracks (range ~3–5 cm = ~2–3 cubes) at all angles
- Three-axis fiber readout gives full 3D track reconstruction including perpendicular and backward-going tracks — directly addressing the ≥25% efficiency at all angles requirement
- Plastic scintillator (C₈H₈) has ~7.7% H nucleon fraction — this **exceeds** the 2% limit, so the scintillator must be replaced or heavily diluted

**Resolution of H constraint:** The cube array must use a **low-hydrogen or hydrogen-free scintillator**, or more practically, the target must be predominantly a high-A material. The standard solution for ≤2% H is to use the scintillator as a **minority fraction** embedded in a heavier matrix, OR to use **gadolinium-doped or lead-doped** panels, OR to design the target as alternating thin scintillator planes with thick carbon/iron absorber slabs. However, if the goal is an *active* neutrino interaction target (not a sampling calorimeter), the preferred modern solution is:

- **Carbon-dominant target:** Use graphite or carbon plates as the primary target material, with thin scintillator planes interleaved. Carbon has 0% H; thin scintillator layers contribute <2% H nucleons overall.
- Alternatively, a **liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC)** satisfies the H constraint (zero hydrogen) and provides the required granularity, but the volume (~6 m³) and the near-detector high-rate environment make LArTPC technically challenging.

**Most practical modern solution matching all constraints:** A **SuperFGD-type 3D scintillating fiber/cube detector** with the cube composition adjusted — specifically, using polystyrene cubes interspersed with carbon plates such that total H nucleon fraction ≤2%. The active target is a *sampling* active target.

---

### 2. Surrounding Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) on the lateral faces

**Technology:** High-pressure gaseous Ar TPCs (or low-mass wire/pad TPCs with Ar:CF₄ or Ar:isobutane gas), placed on the four sides (top, bottom, left, right) and the upstream face of the active target volume.

**Why:**
- Tracks exiting sideways or backward from the active target enter these TPCs for momentum measurement by curvature in the dipole field
- The existing downstream drift chambers handle forward tracks; the lateral TPCs close the acceptance gap for perpendicular and backward tracks, achieving the required ≥25% muon reconstruction efficiency at all angles
- TPCs provide dE/dx particle identification, helping distinguish muons from protons at low momentum
- Low-mass construction minimizes secondary interactions and multiple scattering

---

### 3. Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECal) surrounding the TPC/target system

**Technology:** Lead–scintillator sampling calorimeter with WLS fiber readout and SiPM sensors, segmented in 3D, surrounding the lateral TPCs on all six faces.

**Why:**
- Captures photons from π⁰ decay and electrons for background rejection
- Provides energy containment for electromagnetic showers from interactions in the active target
- Needed for full event reconstruction and to separate NC π⁰ backgrounds from signal
- SiPMs are compatible with the modest magnetic field environment

---

### 4. Upgraded Downstream Spectrometer: Additional drift chamber stations and improved electronics

**Technology:** Additional drift chamber planes with smaller cell size and updated front-end ASICs with faster shaping time and higher rate capability (e.g., AFTER/AGET-based electronics).

**Why:**
- Near-detector environment has very high neutrino interaction rate; existing chambers may have occupancy and pile-up issues
- Higher rate electronics reduce track-merging inefficiency for forward-going muons
- Additional stations improve pattern recognition for the high-multiplicity events expected at 410 m from target

---

### 5. Scintillator Muon Range Detector (MRD) / Downstream stopping muon catcher

**Technology:** Interleaved iron plates and scintillator bars (or scintillator paddles with SiPMs), placed downstream of the existing drift chambers.

**Why:**
- Many muons from 0.7 GeV neutrino interactions stop before exiting the downstream spectrometer
- A range stack measures momentum of stopping muons from range rather than curvature, extending acceptance to low-momentum muons that do not give a reliable curvature measurement
- Iron–scintillator MRD is a proven, cost-effective technology for this role (used in e.g. SciBooNE, T2K ND280)

---

### 6. Beam timing and trigger system: Fine-grained timing with ~1 ns resolution

Before proposing upgrades, let me work through the constraints:

**Muon reconstruction:** Need ≥25% efficiency at *all* angles including 90° and backward-going. This rules out purely tracking-based detectors with strong forward bias. The 0.15 T magnet over 6.5 m gives a momentum kick of ~0.9 GeV/c (p⊥ = 0.3·B·L = 0.3 × 0.15 × 6.5 ≈ 0.29 GeV/c sagitta-equivalent; actually BdL = 0.975 T·m, so maximum bend angle for a straight track ~0.3·0.975/p). Tracks exiting transversely escape the downstream gas drift chambers, so the active target itself must provide momentum measurement for large-angle and backward tracks.

**Proton reconstruction:** 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has range ~12 mm in water (ρ=1 g/cm³) or ~3–4 mm in iron. This demands fine-grained, low-Z material with millimeter-scale spatial resolution. A 60 MeV proton has momentum ~340 MeV/c and range in liquid scintillator (~0.86 g/cm³) of roughly 15 mm. The tracking pitch must be well below this.

**Hydrogen constraint:** ≤2% hydrogen nucleons as fraction of total nucleons. For comparison:
- Pure CH₂ (polyethylene): ~14/16 = ~57% H by nucleon count — far too high
- Liquid argon: 0% H — excellent but no H signal to subtract
- Water (H₂O): 2/18 × 100% ≈ 11% — too high
- Polystyrene (CH): ~8% H by nucleon — too high
- Pure carbon (graphite): 0% H
- Iron: 0% H

If the active target contains any organic material, the hydrogen fraction must be controlled. For scintillator-based detectors, one must heavily dilute hydrogen-containing components with high-A material.

For a mixture with mass fraction f_H in hydrogen-containing material embedded in high-A absorber:
Nucleon fraction of H ≈ (f·ρ_scint·(H nucleons/molecule))/(total nucleon density)

A practical bound: if scintillator fills fraction φ of volume and the rest is e.g. iron or lead:
N_H/N_total ≤ 0.02 → constrains φ severely.

For polystyrene scintillator (C₈H₈, ~8 H per 104 amu): H nucleon fraction in pure scintillator ≈ 8/104 ≈ 7.7%. To dilute to 2%: need φ_scint ≤ 0.02/0.077 ≈ 26% by mass in a zero-H absorber. This is achievable with a sampling calorimeter structure.

Alternatively, use a liquid argon or gaseous target — zero hydrogen, but then no H subtraction needed (and no H contamination problem), though the physics case may require some H for cross-section ratio measurements.

The upstream veto planes, normally used to reject beam-unrelated muons entering from outside, are repurposed in trigger logic as *backward muon detectors*. With a time-of-flight signature (hit upstream *after* a vertex in the cube array) and the beam-spill timing, backward muons are tagged with high efficiency.
- **Michel electron tagging:** Stopped muons in or near the active target decay to Michel electrons (~50 MeV). Identifying the 2.2 μs delayed Michel electron in these planes tags muon stops, providing a nearly pure CC-event sample and a momentum cross-check for low-momentum muons that range out.
- **Side-exiting track efficiency:** Tracks at 90° exit through the 2.6 m or 2.3 m side faces. Scintillator strip planes on these faces catch the exiting track and provide at least one additional measured hit, satisfying the minimum reconstruction requirement even when only a stub is in the cube array.

## Upgrade 5: SiPM-Based Timing Upgrade to Existing Drift Chambers

**Technology:** Replace or supplement existing drift-chamber front-end electronics with waveform-digitizing ASICs (e.g., DREAM/ROC style) providing ~1 ns timing resolution; add a T0 reference scintillator plane at the downstream end of the magnet.

**Physics motivation:**

- **Multi-track disambiguation:** At 0.7 GeV peak energy, neutrino interactions produce several charged secondaries. Drift chambers with ~100 ns integration windows cannot separate tracks from the same interaction that are spatially close. Sub-nanosecond timing resolves this ambiguity.
- **Beam-background rejection:** The near-station beam spill structure at an accelerator means the detector sees a high rate of beam-related muons. Precise timing separates the prompt neutrino interaction products from delayed secondaries or accidental coincidences, reducing backgrounds to the backward-muon sample in particular.
- **Charge-sign crosscheck via curvature:** Better hit timing improves left-right ambiguity resolution in the drift cells, directly improving momentum resolution for tracks that cross only a few cells — namely the large-angle tracks of interest.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context and Constraints

The detector needs to: (1) reconstruct muons at all angles including backward-going with ≥25% efficiency, (2) reconstruct low-energy recoil protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy, (3) keep hydrogen fraction ≤2% of target nucleons, and (4) function inside a 0.15 T dipole field in a ~2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m active volume.

---

## Upgrade 1: Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) — *Rejected on hydrogen constraint*

Before proposing the primary technology, it is worth noting why a LArTPC is **not** the right choice here. Liquid argon has no free hydrogen (hydrogen fraction in Ar is 0%), so the hydrogen-subtraction model is irrelevant — but the physics motivation for the analysis *requires* hydrogen to be present and subtractable. More critically, a LArTPC cannot be built with controllable hydrogen content tuned to ~2%. It is excluded by the problem's own constraint structure.

---

## Upgrade 1: Plastic Scintillator 3D-Granular Active Target

**Technology:** Finely segmented plastic scintillator cubes (e.g., ~1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm polystyrene cubes with embedded WLS fibers read out by SiPMs on three orthogonal faces), following the SuperFGD concept demonstrated for T2K.

**Physics motivation:**

- **Hydrogen content control:** Polystyrene (C₈H₈) has a hydrogen mass fraction of ~7.7%, giving a hydrogen-to-nucleon ratio well above 2%. This is too high on its own, so the cubes would need to be interspersed with or partially replaced by carbon-rich or higher-Z inserts (see Upgrade 2). However, the plastic matrix sets the ceiling, and mixing in denser material brings the free-hydrogen fraction down to the ≤2% requirement while retaining sensitivity.
- **4π track reconstruction:** The 3D-granular geometry breaks the conventional planar-TPC limitation. A proton stopping in a 1.5 cm cube deposits ~1–2 MeV, giving visible tracks for protons with kinetic energy as low as ~5 MeV — well below the 60 MeV requirement. Backward-going and sideways muons traverse multiple cubes and are reconstructed without geometric acceptance gaps.
- **Recoil proton reconstruction:** Short proton tracks (60 MeV kinetic energy → range ~1.5 cm in plastic) cross approximately 1–2 cube widths, producing a chain of hits that can be identified by dE/dx and range. The fine segmentation is essential; a coarser geometry would lose these tracks entirely.
- **Charge reconstruction in the magnet:** Tracks leaving the active target volume enter the downstream drift chambers. The granular target provides the upstream seed trajectory for curvature measurement in the 0.15 T field.

---

## Upgrade 2: Mixed-Composition Target Inserts to Control Hydrogen Fraction

**Technology:** Periodic insertion of thin carbon graphite or aluminum plates (or water/hydrocarbon bags) alternating with the scintillator cubes. A water-layer option (using thin-walled acrylic cells ~3 mm thick) allows in-situ subtraction of oxygen-nucleus interactions and tuning of the H fraction. Alternatively, replacing some plastic cubes with polystyrene cubes doped with high-density filler (e.g., Bi₂O₃ powder embedded in the scintillator matrix) reduces the volumetric hydrogen fraction.

**Physics motivation:**

- **Hydrogen fraction ≤2% requirement:** Pure polystyrene has ~7.7% hydrogen by mass; to bring the free-hydrogen nucleon fraction to ≤2% while maintaining scintillation, one must dilute the hydrogen content. With ~75% of the volume replaced by carbon inserts (density ~2.2 g/cm³ vs. ~1.05 g/cm³ for plastic), the blended target reaches the required composition. Exact tuning is straightforward at the design stage.
- **Interaction-target control:** Having separate carbon/water sub-targets within the same active volume allows the analysis to statistically subtract non-hydrogen interactions using different data samples collected simultaneously, improving the hydrogen-extraction model's robustness.
- **Mechanical compatibility:** Thin graphite or metal sheets interleaved with scintillator cubes are mechanically straightforward, do not require cryogenics, and fit within the existing 0.9 m depth along the beam.

---

## Upgrade 3: High-Granularity Silicon Pixel Tracker Planes

**Technology:** Thin MAPS (Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor) silicon pixel planes, ~50–100 µm thick per layer, with ~100 µm pitch, placed at ~5–10 cm intervals throughout the active volume. Similar to the ALICE ITS3 or DUNE ND-LAr vertex tracker concepts.

**Physics motivation:**

- **Vertex resolution for interaction-point determination:** With a granular scintillator target, the vertex position is known to ~1 cube width (~1.5 cm). Silicon pixel planes inserted at regular intervals improve the vertex resolution to ~100–200 µm, critical for separating the neutrino interaction vertex from secondary interactions (re-interactions of the recoil proton, pion production).
- **Backward-going muon efficiency:** A muon emitted at 90°–180° to the beam immediately exits the upstream face of the active volume. Silicon planes upstream of the scintillator (covering the full 2.6 × 2.3 m² cross-section) catch these tracks within the first centimeter of travel and provide the seed hits needed to trigger reconstruction and satisfy the ≥25% efficiency requirement at all angles.
- **Low-mass material budget:** At ~0.1% X₀ per layer, silicon planes contribute negligible multiple scattering for proton and muon tracks — unlike adding more scintillator or gas layers. This preserves angular resolution for low-momentum tracks.
- **dE/dx particle ID:** Silicon pixel planes provide energy-loss measurements that complement the scintillator's light yield, improving π/p/µ separation for tracks too short to be identified by range alone.

---

## Upgrade 4: Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes at the Active Volume Boundaries

**Technology:** Fast plastic scintillator panels (e.g., EJ-200 or BC-404) ~1 cm thick with SiPM readout, achieving ~200–300 ps time resolution, placed on all six faces of the active target volume (upstream, downstream, top, bottom, left, right).

**Physics motivation:**

- **Backward-going track identification:** A muon emitted backward exits the upstream face before the downstream face. With ~200 ps timing, a 500 MeV/c muon traversing 90 cm is tagged unambiguously by the upstream-face ToF panel firing before any downstream panel — directly fulfilling the backward-track reconstruction requirement.
- **Sideways muon reconstruction:** Muons leaving through the lateral faces (perpendicular tracks) are caught by the side ToF panels. The timing combined with the entry point in the scintillator provides a rough momentum estimate from track length even before the drift chamber measurement.
- **Neutron rejection:** Neutrino interactions produce neutrons that can re-interact inside the volume and mimic proton tracks. ToF allows neutrons (which travel at β < 1) to be distinguished from protons and pions, cleaning up the recoil-proton sample particularly at low kinetic energies near the 60 MeV threshold.
- **Beam-out-of-time background rejection:** The 200–300 ps resolution is well-matched to the accelerator's RF bucket structure, allowing cosmic ray and beam-unrelated backgrounds to be vetoed.

---

## Upgrade 5: Replacement or Augmentation of Drift Chambers with µRWELL or Small-Tube Straw Tracker

**Technology:** Micro-Resistive Well (µRWELL) detector planes or 5 mm-diameter straw-tube drift chambers replacing or supplementing the existing downstream gas drift chambers.

**Physics motivation:**

- **Improved angular coverage for muons from large-angle interactions:** The existing drift chambers were presumably optimized for forward-going tracks. Large-angle muons from sideways and backward interactions enter the drift chambers at oblique angles, reducing position resolution and hit efficiency. µRWELL planes provide 2D position measurement with ~100 µm resolution at any track angle, with no geometric dead zones at large incidence angles.
- **Radiation hardness and rate capability:** µRWELL detectors tolerate higher particle fluxes than conventional wire chambers, relevant as beam intensity may increase in future runs. Their resistive layer suppresses discharges.
- **Charge-sign determination:** The analysis requires muon charge (to separate ν_µ from ν̄_µ interactions). Improving momentum resolution in the downstream spectrometer reduces the fraction of tracks whose curvature is poorly measured, increasing the effective statistics of the charge-signed sample at large angles where the lever arm in the 0.15 T field is shorter.
- **Operation in the stray field:** µRWELL and straw tubes are robust in modest magnetic fields, unlike some earlier wire-chamber designs where the 0.15 T fringe field at the chamber edges degraded performance.

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Replace Passive Target with a 3D Scintillator Cube Array (Primary Recommendation)

Replace the existing passive target material with an array of **small plastic scintillator cubes** (e.g., 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm) read out on three orthogonal faces by **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres** threaded through each cube, following the SuperFGD/SND@LHC design heritage.

- **Granularity**: 1.5 cm cubes give ~1.5 cm 3D space points, sufficient to resolve 60 MeV proton tracks (~3–4 cubes long)
- **4π tracking**: Isotropic hit pattern means no geometric acceptance hole for any track angle, satisfying the perpendicular and backward-going muon requirement
- **Low density**: ~1.0 g/cm³, comparable to water; protons range out in a reconstructable number of cubes
- **Scintillation timing** (~1 ns) distinguishes forward from backward-going tracks via time-of-flight across the volume and resolves multiple interaction vertices per spill

**Hydrogen content concern**: Polystyrene (C₈H₈) has ~7.7% hydrogen by nucleon count — far above the 2% limit. This is addressed in item 3 below.

---

### 2. Add Thin Time-Projection Chambers (TPCs) Interleaved with Scintillator Modules

Insert **gaseous TPCs** (e.g., Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ or pure Ar with Micromegas/GEM readout) as thin active layers interleaved every ~15–20 cm through the target volume in the transverse (XY) planes.

- Provide **continuous 3D track reconstruction** with dE/dx particle identification
- Gas medium has negligible hydrogen fraction (~0% for pure Ar, controllable)
- **Charge sign** of short tracks measured from curvature within the magnet volume
- Momentum measurement of stopping tracks from range + curvature combination
- TPC drift along the beam axis (Z); 50–100 µm spatial resolution achievable

Practical format: panels of ~2.6 m × 2.3 m active area, ~5–8 cm drift gap, ~12–18 panels fitting within the 0.9 m depth.

---

### 3. Use a Low-Hydrogen or Hydrogen-Controlled Target Configuration

Since the hydrogen constraint (≤2% nucleon fraction) conflicts with plastic scintillator, implement one of two strategies:

**Option A — Carbon/Argon dominant target**: Replace scintillator cubes with **liquid argon mini-TPC cells** or **graphite/carbon absorber slabs** instrumented with thin-film sensors. Pure ⁴⁰Ar or ¹²C targets have zero hydrogen.

**Option B — Composite target with fiducial bookkeeping**: Use the scintillator cube array but restrict the physics fiducial volume to regions bounded by **water or liquid argon target modules** that dominate the nucleon count. Thin scintillator planes serve only as tracking layers (not as the interaction target). Target modules could be:
- Removable **water-filled acrylic cells** (H₂O: ~11% H by nucleon, but ¹⁶O dominates at ~89%; blending with argon panels achieves the ≤2% average)
- **Liquid argon sandwich layers**: argon has zero hydrogen; alternating Ar and thin scintillator readout layers can dilute hydrogen below 2% by mass

Recommend **Option B with water targets** as water has well-understood cross-sections and the hydrogen subtraction model is most mature for H₂O targets.

---

### 4. Upgrade the Surrounding Muon Identification System

The existing drift chambers downstream reconstruct forward muons well, but the new requirement for backward and perpendicular muons demands instrumentation on **all six faces** of the target volume:

- **Upstream face**: Add a 2.6 m × 2.3 m array of scintillator tracking planes (3–4 layers, X–Y stereo) immediately upstream of the target, backed by ~20 cm of iron as a muon range stack
- **Side faces (4 lateral surfaces)**: Add scintillator paddle arrays or resistive plate chambers (RPCs) on the ±X and ±Y faces of the magnet bore; the warm magnet yoke steel can serve as partial muon absorber/range stack
- **Downstream face**: Existing drift chambers retained; add scintillator trigger hodoscope for timing
- **Goal**: Muon identification and momentum-by-range for tracks exiting any face; combined with the magnet field for curvature measurement of tracks that traverse sufficient path length (~30–50 cm in field)

For backward-going muons that stop inside the target volume, **range-based momentum reconstruction** from the cube array hit count is sufficient provided the cube-to-cube light yield is calibrated to ≲5% uniformity.

---

### 5. Add a High-Resolution Timing Layer

Install **fast scintillator timing planes** (e.g., LYSO bars or fast plastic with SiPM readout, σ_t ~ 100–200 ps) on the upstream and downstream faces:

- Resolves ambiguity between forward and backward-going tracks when curvature is small (low-momentum or nearly perpendicular tracks)
- Enables **time-of-flight proton/pion separation** over the ~50 cm scale of the target for momenta up to ~600 MeV/c
- Provides beam-spill pile-up rejection at the ~1 ns level

---

### 6. Electronics and DAQ Upgrade

- Replace triggered readout with **continuous waveform digitisation** at ≥250 MHz sampling on all SiPM channels (target: ~500k channels for full cube array)
- Implement **online FPGA-based clustering** to reduce data rate before storage
- Synchronise timing across subsystems to <1 ns using a White Rabbit or similar precision timing network
- This is essential because the 4π tracking geometry generates complex multi-hit patterns requiring full waveform information for disambiguation

# Design Review: Kestrel Flats Near Station – Active Target Upgrade Recommendations

## Preamble: Deriving the Key Constraints

Before recommending technologies, I work through the physics constraints explicitly.

**Hydrogen fraction constraint:** ≤2% of nucleons may be hydrogen. Carbon has 6 protons + 6 neutrons = 12 nucleons, zero free hydrogen. Pure CH₂ polyethylene has 2H per 14 nucleons = 14.3% — far too high. Polystyrene (C₈H₈) gives 8H per 16 nucleons = 50% — far too high. Pure water (H₂O) gives 2H per 18 nucleons = 11% — too high. Liquid argon has zero free hydrogen. A scintillator like C₁₀H₁₁ (approximate for polyvinyltoluene/PVT-based plastic) gives ~8–9% hydrogen by nucleon count — still too high without dilution. **To achieve ≤2% hydrogen by nucleon fraction, the dominant nuclear target must be a heavy nucleus, or the hydrogen-bearing material must be diluted to <~5% of the total mass.** The natural solution is a high-Z or medium-Z active target where any plastic/organic scintillator is a minority component, **or** a liquid argon or liquid-based TPC where no hydrogen is present at all.

**Angular coverage including backward tracks:** Conventional drift chambers downstream cannot reconstruct backward-going or perpendicular tracks alone. The active target must self-reconstruct such tracks.

**Proton threshold ~60 MeV kinetic energy:** Range in water at 60 MeV ≈ 14 mm; in iron ≈ 3–4 mm; in plastic scintillator ≈ 25 mm. This demands fine spatial granularity — centimeter scale or better — and low-Z enough material that the range is not too short to measure.

**Volume:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m ≈ 5.4 m³, relatively compact.

**Muon reconstruction ≥25% at all angles including 90° and backward:** Track segments must be found and matched to the downstream spectrometer, or the target itself must supply momentum measurement for contained or exiting tracks.

---

## Recommendation 1: Replace the target region with a Straw-Tube Tracker (STT) using argon-CO₂ gas fill and thin radiators

**Technology:** A high-density array of aluminized Mylar straw tubes (~5–7 mm diameter) in X-Y-Z stereo orientations, with thin polypropylene or carbon fiber radiator/support planes interspersed, filling the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume.

**Target nucleon composition:** The dominant nuclear targets are the radiator/support material — using **graphite or pure carbon fiber panels** as thin passive layers between straw planes keeps the nucleon composition almost entirely ¹²C, with negligible hydrogen from the straw walls. Carbon panels of ~3 mm thickness every ~2–3 cm of depth give a fiducial target that is effectively a carbon nucleus target. The gas (Ar:CO₂ 70:30) contributes negligible mass. Hydrogen nucleon fraction from Mylar (C₁₀H₈O₄) straw walls: at typical wall thicknesses of 30–50 μm vs. 3 mm carbon panels, hydrogen nucleons remain well under 2% — this requires careful engineering but is achievable and has been demonstrated by the NINJA/Baby MIND and NOvA near detector programs; the ICARUS and T2K ND280 TPCs provide further precedent.

**Justification for 60 MeV proton threshold:** Straw tubes provide ~200 μm position resolution per hit; a 60 MeV proton has a range of ~24 mm in the gas+radiator composite, crossing several straw layers — measurable if straw pitch is ≤5 mm projected. This is the most demanding constraint and **sets the pitch/diameter of the straws**.

**Justification for angular coverage:** With X, Y, and ±(45°–60°) stereo views repeated throughout the depth, tracks at any polar and azimuthal angle — including those parallel to the beam axis (which cross many stereo straws) and those perpendicular or backward — produce enough hits for reconstruction. The magnet field still acts on tracks leaving the target volume; tracks that stop inside can be range-momentum-measured.

**Justification for muon efficiency:** Even short muon stubs inside the target are reconstructed from multiple straw hits. Backward muons are caught by the upstream stereo planes. The ≥25% efficiency requirement is met because the inefficiency of any single straw (~1–2%) is diluted over many crossings.

---

## Recommendation 2: Instrument the downstream face of the target with a thin scintillating fiber (SciFi) hodoscope wall

**Technology:** 1 mm diameter Kuraray SCSF-78 scintillating fibers in X-Y double layers, read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), forming two planes (one per transverse view) at the downstream boundary of the active target volume.

**Justification:** This provides a precise time and position seed for tracks exiting toward the downstream drift chambers, improving the matching efficiency for forward-going and near-forward muons. The timing resolution of ~1 ns from SiPM readout also suppresses out-of-time backgrounds (cosmic rays, beam halo) which are a known issue at 410 m from the target where neutrino event rates are high. SciFi hodoscopes of this type are mature technology (LHCb SciFi Tracker, T2K INGRID, NA61 vertex detector).

**Hydrogen contribution:** 1 mm SciFi planes are thin enough that their contribution to the nucleon count remains well under the 2% hydrogen budget if the planes are kept to ≤2 planes of 1 mm fiber per meter of depth. This must be tracked in a running materials budget spreadsheet.

---

## Recommendation 3: Add a segmented resistive plate chamber (RPC) or thin-gap TPC layer on the **upstream face** of the active target

**Technology:** 2–3 layers of glass or Bakelite RPCs with ~1 cm strip readout, or thin multi-wire proportional chambers (MWPCs) with cathode strip readout, covering the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m upstream face.

**Justification:** This is specifically to catch **backward-going tracks** — the analysis requirement explicitly names these. A backward muon or backward proton that exits the upstream face would otherwise be lost entirely. These upstream tracking planes provide the necessary hits to seed backward track reconstruction. RPCs are well-proven for large-area muon detection (ATLAS muon system, CMS muon system, OPERA) and can be operated in avalanche mode for the required spatial resolution (~1 cm). Bakelite RPCs contain minimal hydrogen (mostly carbon and oxygen in the polymer backbone), so the hydrogen nucleon budget impact is small for the thin layers proposed.

**Alternative:** If RPC gas mixture (typically C₂H₂F₄/isobutane/SF₆) is a concern for hydrogen, the isobutane fraction can be reduced and the thin-gap geometry chosen to minimize gas mass; or resistive MICROMEGAS detectors on a copper-clad G10 frame can substitute, though G10 epoxy contains some hydrogen requiring accounting.

---

## Recommendation 4: Replace or supplement the existing gas drift chamber readout electronics with a **continuous waveform digitizer** (flash ADC at ≥50 MSPS)

**Technology:** Flash ADC-based readout boards (e.g., similar to the CAEN V1742 / DRS4-based systems, or custom ASICs as used in MicroBooNE and SBND) on all straw-tube and existing drift chamber channels.

**Justification:** At 410 m from the target, the near detector sees a high neutrino interaction rate per spill. Continuous digitization enables offline disambiguation of multiple interactions within a single beam spill, recovery of tracks with delayed hits (e.g., from delta rays, secondary scatters, or Michel electrons from stopped muons), and precise drift-time-to-position conversion without the threshold-setting compromises of leading-edge discriminators. This directly improves reconstruction efficiency for the low-momentum protons at 60 MeV, whose signals are small and whose tracks may be non-linear due to multiple scattering — waveform information provides dE/dx for particle ID as well as improved hit finding.

---

## Recommendation 5: Install a **thin liquid-scintillator neutron veto** layer on all six faces of the active target volume (or at minimum the four transverse faces)

**Technology:** 10–15 cm thick EJ-301 or EJ-335 gadolinium-loaded liquid scintillator (or alternatively BC-521 Gd-loaded plastic) panels, read by PMTs or SiPMs at the edges, providing pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) capability to distinguish neutron captures from gammas and charged particles.

**Justification:** At 60 MeV proton threshold, neutrons from neutrino interactions (knocked-out neutrons from nuclear breakup, or quasi-elastic scattering on neutrons) can mimic short proton tracks or cause secondary interactions that contaminate the sample. The veto layers tag neutrons escaping the active volume (by detecting their eventual capture on Gd with the characteristic 8 MeV gamma cascade), enabling a neutron-multiplicity measurement that constrains nuclear interaction models. Gadolinium loading (0.1% by mass) captures thermal neutrons within ~20 μs with high efficiency. This is established technology (Daya Bay, RENO, Double Chooz all use Gd-loaded liquid scintillator; neutron tagging in near detectors is used by T2K ND280 and MINERvA). The hydrogen content of the veto panels does not count toward the 2% budget if the veto is treated as outside the fiducial volume, but this boundary must be defined carefully in the analysis.

---

## Recommendation 6: Upgrade the magnet power supply and monitoring to enable **polarity reversal on a spill-by-spill basis**

**Technology:** Reversible bipolar power supply (H-bridge configuration, standard industrial components for warm magnets of this current range, ~few kA) with interlocks and fast-switching capability (reversal in <1 spill cycle, typically ≤seconds for warm magnets of this scale).

**Justification:** The charge asymmetry between μ⁺ and μ⁻ (from ν_μ vs. ν̄_μ interactions) is a critical cross-section measurement. By running equal numbers of spills in each polarity, systematic uncertainties from the magnetic field map and from left-right asymmetries in the drift chamber geometry cancel to first order. This is a low-cost electronics and infrastructure change to what is presumably a DC-powered warm magnet, and it is standard practice in experiments of this type (e.g., MINERvA, MINOS near detector). It also allows the sign of tracks that stop inside the active target (and thus cannot be bent into the downstream spectrometer) to be inferred statistically.

## Critical Design Warning

The hydrogen nucleon fraction budget is the tightest constraint and must be enforced with a formal materials accounting system updated at every design change. Every component inside the fiducial volume — straw walls, adhesives, gas seals, support ribs, circuit boards on in-volume electronics — must be assayed for hydrogen content and entered into a running total. Historical experience (MINERvA, NOvA) shows that hydrogen accumulates in "invisible" components (glues, coatings, PCB substrates) and can silently violate the budget. I recommend appointing a dedicated materials officer with veto authority over any in-volume component change.

**Technology: Plastic scintillator cubes (~1.5 cm side) read out by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers in three orthogonal views (SuperFGD-style)**

## Upgrade 1: 3D Scintillator Cube Active Target

**Technology:** Fully-active plastic scintillator cube array (e.g., 1–1.5 cm³ optically-isolated cubes read out by wavelength-shifting fibers through two or three faces, as demonstrated by the SuperFGD prototype).

**Physics motivation:**

The 90°-and-backward muon requirement immediately kills any detector geometry that is segmented only in the beam direction. Conventional scintillator planes (like a fine-grained tracker built from XY planes) have track-length thresholds and angular acceptance holes near 90° because a track traverses minimal active material and maximal dead material at that angle. A cubic 3D lattice has no preferred axis: a track at any angle traverses a path length through active scintillator that is essentially independent of angle (varying only as the chord length through a cube), so efficiency is geometrically uniform.

For the 60 MeV kinetic energy proton, the range in polystyrene is roughly 3 cm, meaning the track crosses only ~2–3 cubes. This is detectable if each cube is individually read out, which the WLS-fiber-through-face scheme provides. A conventional drift chamber or TPC would not contain these tracks within a fiducial volume and would suffer from reconstruction ambiguities; the cube array reconstructs short, highly-ionizing stubs unambiguously via the high dE/dx signal in neighboring cubes.

The hydrogen content of polystyrene (C₈H₈) is about 7.7% by mass, giving a hydrogen-to-nucleon ratio near 7–8%, far above the 2% limit. Therefore the cubes must be made of a low-hydrogen or hydrogen-free scintillator, or a composite. Options include:

- **Carbon-loaded or graphite-fiber composite scintillator** tiles
- **Liquid-argon or gas-filled cells** (but these complicate construction)
- **Polystyrene cubes interspersed with passive high-A absorber layers** in a ratio that dilutes the hydrogen fraction to ≤ 2% — but this reduces the active fraction and defeats short-track detection.

The cleanest path is **substituting the polystyrene with a heavier scintillating medium** (e.g., lead-loaded scintillator, or gadolinium-doped scintillator tiles with thin profiles) or choosing a geometry in which thin plastic scintillator layers alternate with passive argon or iron at a ratio that keeps hydrogen nucleons below 2%. The 3D cube architecture directly addresses the 4π angular requirement and the short-track requirement simultaneously, making it the cornerstone upgrade.

- **Sign determination for backward muons:** A backward muon that re-enters the magnet volume from upstream traverses the TPC panels on the upstream face; charge-sign measurement in the fringe field requires at least a few measured space-points before the track exits the magnet bore.
- **Matching to downstream drift chambers:** A continuous track from the cube array through the TPC panels into the downstream drift chambers gives an unambiguous momentum measurement via curvature.
- **Low-mass construction:** Gas TPCs contribute minimal material (≪1% X₀ per panel), so they do not degrade the energy reconstruction of particles stopping in or near the active target.
- **Hydrogen contribution negligible:** Gas-volume hydrogen content is negligible at atmospheric pressure.

Liquid argon meets all three conditions. Argon is 0% hydrogen, which keeps the hydrogen fraction far below 2% and also suits a hydrogen-free far detector.

## Recommended hardware

**1. Modular, pixelated liquid-argon TPC filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region**
- **Statistics:** about 5.4 m³ of liquid argon is roughly 7 t, far more target mass than a gas TPC.
- **3D pixel readout (about 3–4 mm pitch) instead of wire planes:**
  - Gives true 3D imaging, with no ambiguity for tracks parallel to a wire plane or perpendicular to the beam.
  - Copes with pile-up at 410 m from the target, where several interactions per spill are likely in a 7 t target. This follows the ArgonCube/ND-LAr design.
- **Short drift lengths (modular cells of about 0.5 m):** this keeps diffusion, space-charge and purity demands low, which matters in a confined volume inside a warm magnet.
- **Proton detection:** a 60 MeV proton travels roughly 2–3 cm in liquid argon, so it leaves about 6–10 pixel hits in any direction. dE/dx gives proton/pion identification, giving full-angle acceptance down to the required threshold.

**2. Segmented optical readout inside each module (for example, light traps or ArCLight-type tiles)**
- Provides the interaction time (t0) and absolute drift-coordinate reconstruction.
- Matches charge to individual interactions within a spill.
- Gives timing that helps separate backward-going from forward-going tracks.

**3. Thin, vacuum-insulated cryostat shaped to fit the 0.9 m depth inside the magnet**
- Minimises dead material, so that:
  - low-energy particles are not lost;
  - tracks can reach outer detectors with little multiple scattering.
- Avoids thick hydrogen-rich foam insulation near the fiducial volume. Material outside the active volume does not count toward target nucleons, but interactions in it must be rejectable by fiducial cuts.

**4. Tracking and time-of-flight panels on the upstream, top, bottom and side faces of the target**
- **Why:** the existing drift chambers sit only downstream, so muons at about 90° or going backward never reach them.
- **Proposed technology:**
  - Thin gas tracker planes, such as resistive Micromegas or small TPC/drift modules, for curvature in the 0.15 T field.
  - Fast scintillator time-of-flight bars (about 100–150 ps) to decide track direction and charge sense.
- **Hydrogen:** these panels sit outside the target fiducial volume, so they do not affect the hydrogen fraction.
- This is what secures at least 25% muon efficiency at all angles.

**5. Momentum estimation from inside the liquid argon for tracks that never reach a tracker**
- Use range for stopping tracks. A 0.7 GeV-beam muon of a few hundred MeV ranges about 1 m in liquid argon.
- Use multiple-Coulomb-scattering fits for exiting tracks.
- This needs the fine pixel granularity and readout electronics with enough dynamic range and low noise (cold ASICs).

**6. Supporting infrastructure**
- **Argon purification and recirculation:** needed to keep electron lifetime well above the drift time.
- **Cryogenic services routed through the magnet:** the warm dipole limits access, so these need to be planned at the proposal stage.
- **Calibration systems:**
  - laser or cosmic-ray calibration of the drift field and dE/dx;
  - charge calibration for proton identification.

## Why not the alternatives

- **Plastic, water or organic scintillator:** too much hydrogen, as shown above.
- **High-pressure argon gas TPC:** acceptable for hydrogen if a hydrogen-free quencher such as CF₄ is used, and it gives an excellent proton threshold. However, at about 10 bar the target mass is only around 100 kg. It is a possible complementary option, not the main target.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a modular pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (hydrogen-free, ~7 t, isotropic 3D tracking down to ~60 MeV protons), since plastic scintillator's ~7.7% hydrogen violates the 2% limit.

# Design Review Recommendations: Kestrel Flats Near Station Active Target Upgrade

## Analysis of Requirements

Before recommending hardware, I'll derive the key constraints:

**Magnetic analysis:** B = 0.15 T over L = 6.5 m gives BL = 0.975 T·m. For a 300 MeV/c muon (typical near-peak), sagitta ≈ 0.3BL²/p ≈ 1.5 cm — measurable, but barely. Backward and transverse tracks may not reach the downstream drift chambers at all, so **the active target itself must provide tracking and momentum measurement for contained or large-angle tracks.**

**Proton range:** A proton with KE = 60 MeV has range in water ~15 mm, in scintillator ~18 mm, in argon ~25 mm. The detector must have fine enough segmentation to reconstruct these short tracks with sufficient points for dE/dx identification.

**Hydrogen constraint:** ≤2% hydrogen nucleons means the dominant target material must be low-H or H-free. Pure water (~11% H by nucleon count), plastic scintillator (CH, ~7.7% H), and liquid argon (0% H) differ critically here.

**Volume:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m = ~5.4 m³, so the technology must be scalable.

**Angular coverage:** 4π tracking including backward tracks eliminates projective-only detector geometries.

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. Replace the existing passive target with a low-gain Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) — *Primary Active Target*

**Technology:** Modular LArTPC with wire or pixel readout, operating in the existing magnetic volume.

**Justification:**

- Liquid argon contains **zero hydrogen**, trivially satisfying the ≤2% H constraint (H/nucleon = 0).
- LAr has density ~1.4 g/cm³ and an intrinsic spatial resolution of O(1 mm) with wire readout (3 mm wire pitch gives ~1 mm resolution along drift), comfortably tracking 60 MeV protons whose ~25 mm range gives ~25 measurable points.
- The continuous-readout, fully 3D imaging nature of a LArTPC provides inherent 4π track reconstruction, satisfying the backward and transverse muon requirement.
- dE/dx from charge deposition allows proton/pion/muon separation track-by-track.
- The 0.9 m depth along beam fits within practical drift distances for a single-drift or dual-drift TPC with HV of ~90–180 kV (at 500 V/cm), which is achievable with commercial HV systems.
- **Concern/mitigation:** The warm dipole field (0.15 T) complicates electron drift in a LArTPC if the electric and magnetic fields are not aligned. The E×B distortion causes the drift to deviate, but with careful orientation of the TPC drift direction **parallel to the magnetic field** (i.e., drift along the magnet axis, with wires reading the transverse plane), the Lorentz angle is small and correctable. Alternatively, use a **pixelated charge readout (LArPix-style)** which is field-direction-agnostic and provides true 3D hits without ambiguity from wire projections — preferable given the 4π tracking requirement.

**Specific sub-recommendation:** Use **LArPix pixel readout** tiles on the anode planes rather than wire planes. This eliminates projection ambiguities for high-multiplicity events, is insensitive to the magnetic field orientation issue, and gives genuine 3D hit positions at ~4 mm pitch (current LArPix generation), sufficient for the proton tracking requirement.

---

### 2. Add a surrounding scintillator veto/tagger array — *Muon Range Stack and Containment Monitor*

**Technology:** Extruded plastic scintillator bars (e.g., Fermilab-style 3.3 × 4.1 cm² cross-section bars with WLS fiber and SiPM readout), arrayed on all six faces of the active volume.

**Justification:**

- Muons that **exit** the LArTPC — particularly forward-going high-energy muons — must be matched to the downstream drift chambers. The scintillator layer on the downstream face provides a precise exit-point measurement and a trigger signal for the matching, recovering efficiency for these tracks.
- Backward-going muons (against the beam) will stop in the scintillator on the upstream face or be tracked through it; the scintillator provides range-based momentum estimation for muons that stop within or just outside the LArTPC, supplementing the magnetic spectrometer for contained tracks.
- Transverse (90°) muons exit through the side faces and would otherwise not reach the downstream drift chambers; the side scintillator panels extend their tracking volume and provide at least a range constraint.
- The 25% minimum efficiency requirement at **all angles** is thus met by: (a) LArTPC internal tracking for short/contained tracks, (b) scintillator+drift chamber for forward tracks, (c) scintillator range stack for side/backward muons that stop nearby.
- Plastic scintillator (CH composition) has ~7.7% hydrogen nucleons. However, this is a **surrounding** detector, not the interaction target. If neutrino interaction vertices are fiducialized 5–10 cm inside the LArTPC boundary, the scintillator contributes negligibly to the analyzed target mass, keeping H well below 2%. This must be enforced at the analysis level with a fiducial cut, which is standard practice.
- SiPM readout operates without issue in the 0.15 T field (unlike PMTs).

---

### 3. Replace or augment the upstream face with a thin upstream tracker — *Beam-entrance tracking plane*

**Technology:** Two planes of silicon strip detectors or scintillating fiber tracker (SciFi, as used in T2K's SFGD predecessor work and LHCb Upgrade), 1–2 mm pitch, covering the full 2.6 × 2.3 m² aperture.

**Justification:**

- Neutrino interactions produce no beam particle track to trigger on, but incoming muon-neutrino interactions can be distinguished from dirt backgrounds (interactions upstream of the detector that send particles in). A thin tracker at the upstream face with high granularity identifies charged particles **entering** the fiducial volume from upstream, flagging backgrounds.
- SciFi planes (~250 µm fiber diameter, grouped to ~1 mm effective pitch) add ~0.5% X₀ per plane — negligible effect on the 60 MeV proton tracks that originate inside the LAr.
- Provides a time reference (SiPM-on-fiber timing ~1 ns resolution) useful for in-time background rejection.
- Contributes zero additional hydrogen to the neutrino target if treated as a veto/tag rather than a fiducial volume.

---

### 4. Upgrade the gas drift chambers' readout electronics — *High-rate, dead-time-free DAQ*

**Technology:** Continuous waveform sampling ASICs (e.g., SAMPA chip as used in ALICE TPC, or equivalent) replacing any existing gated/triggered readout on the downstream drift chambers.

**Justification:**

- The LArTPC and scintillator system will generate data continuously with no hardware trigger. The downstream drift chambers must match this paradigm to enable offline matching of LArTPC-reconstructed tracks to chamber-measured momenta for forward muons.
- Current near-detector beams operate at MHz interaction rates in the target; triggered readout with microsecond dead times loses events. Continuous readout with ~25 ns sampling retains all crossings.
- This is a low-cost electronics-only upgrade that removes a bottleneck created by all the other hardware improvements.

---

### 5. Install a downstream electromagnetic calorimeter sandwich — *Photon and π⁰ reconstruction*

**Technology:** Lead–scintillator sampling calorimeter, 15–20 X₀ deep, ~5 × 5 cm² transverse segmentation, covering the downstream face of the magnet volume.

**Justification:**

- Neutral pions from hadronic recoil systems decay to photon pairs; without downstream EM calorimetry, these are invisible, creating a systematic bias in the reconstructed hadronic recoil and thus in the neutrino energy estimator.
- The LArTPC itself will convert some photons (~18% in ~40 cm LAr), but many will exit downstream. The calorimeter catches these.
- Lead–scintillator with SiPM readout operates in the fringe field downstream of the magnet without issue.
- 5 × 5 cm² cells give ~1° angular resolution at 1 m distance, adequate for π⁰ mass reconstruction.

---

## Summary Table

| Recommendation | Technology | Key Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target replacement | LArTPC with LArPix pixel readout | 4π tracking, 60 MeV protons, H<2% |
| Surrounding scintillator | Extruded scintillator + SiPM | 25% muon efficiency at all angles |
| Upstream tracker | Scintillating fiber planes | Background rejection, beam-entrance tagging |
| Chamber electronics upgrade | Continuous waveform ASIC | Dead-time-free matching to spectrometer |
| Downstream EM calorimeter | Pb-scintillator + SiPM | π⁰ reconstruction, hadronic recoil |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target with a pixelated-readout LArTPC (LArPix-style anode tiles), as it simultaneously satisfies the hydrogen-fraction constraint, enables 4π reconstruction of both short proton tracks and large-angle/backward muons, and provides dE/dx-based particle identification — addressing more of the stated requirements than any other single change.
